report.releaseDate: Annual Report 2025/26 published on singaporepools.com.sg on or before 13 Oct 2026 (exact release date unverified; FY ended 31 Mar 2026)
report.currency: SGD (S$) — tables in S$ millions unless marked bn; company is unlisted and reports annually only (no quarterly/H1 data exist)
report.verdict: A third straight record year — turnover +6.2% to S$13.48bn with growth re-accelerating from +4% and no mega sporting event in the period — but the incremental dollar went almost entirely to prizes, opex and the Exchequer: betting duties & taxes rose 9% to S$2.49bn while the Tote Board contribution (the only "earnings" line the entity reports) was flat at S$583m (+1.4%). For sector investors the read-through is a still-growing Singapore gambling wallet and a monopoly lottery/tote model where the state captures ~88% of implied gross win before costs; this is a fiscal instrument first and an operating business second, and it discloses accordingly.
summary: **Record FY26 turnover with growth re-accelerating.** Stakes rose 6.2% YoY to S$13.48bn (Gaming Intelligence: "+6% to S$13.48bn"; company website "At a Glance" sourced to Annual Report 2025/26: S$13.5bn), following +4.0% in FY25 (S$12.69bn) and +7.0% in FY24 (S$12.2bn). Third consecutive record; 3-year CAGR from FY23's S$11.4bn is 5.7%.

**There are no "expectations" to beat.** Singapore Pools (Private) Limited is unlisted, wholly owned by the Tote Board (a statutory board under the Ministry of Finance), gives no guidance and has no consensus. The only benchmarks are the prior-year trend and the Budget's betting-duty line; against trend, +6% sits at the top of the post-reopening run-rate (ex the FY23 reopening/Qatar World Cup year).

**The state was the main beneficiary of the growth.** Betting duties & taxes rose 9.2% to S$2.49bn (FY25: flat at S$2.28bn), lifting the effective rate to 18.5% of turnover (+50bps). On the incremental S$790m of turnover, ~27c per S$1 went to duties versus an 18c blended average — consistent with mix reverting toward higher-duty lottery products after a sports/racing-led FY25, although the product split is not disclosed [inference, unverified].

**The Tote Board contribution — the entity's de facto earnings line — stalled.** S$583m, +1.4% YoY (FY25: +32% to S$575m; FY24: S$437m), or 4.3% of turnover (−20bps). Incremental flow-through to the surplus line collapsed to ~1c per incremental S$1 of turnover, versus ~28c in FY25.

**FY26 prize payouts and operating expenses are not yet verified.** The residual after duties and Tote Board contribution is S$10.41bn, exactly 77.2% of turnover — identical to FY25 (S$9.45bn prizes + S$353m opex = 77.2%). If opex held near the company's "~3%" framing (~S$0.37–0.40bn), prize payouts were ≈S$10.0bn (~74–74.5% payout ratio vs 74.5% in FY25) [derived estimate].

**Implied gross win ≈S$3.45–3.47bn (+6–7% YoY)** [derived: turnover less estimated prizes]. On that base, duties & taxes absorb ~72% and the Tote Board contribution ~17% — i.e. ~88% of gross win is captured by the state before operating costs. No commercial operator in our coverage runs anything close to this effective rate; it frames why opex discipline (~3% of stakes) is existential rather than optional.

**The "97% returned to Singapore" narrative is intact.** Prizes + duties + Tote Board contribution ≈S$13.1bn in FY26 [derived], after S$12.3bn (97.0%) in FY25 and S$11.87bn (97.3%) in FY24. Management has used this framing in every joint Chairman/CEO message since at least FY24.

**Segment disclosure is nil — do not expect sportsbook KPIs.** The company reports as a single entity across lottery (TOTO, 4D, Singapore Sweep), sports betting (football, motor racing) and horse racing (overseas simulcast). No handle, hold, net/structural margin, promo intensity, actives or ARPU are disclosed; our segment section is therefore built on the distribution waterfall plus qualitative product commentary from the FY24/FY25 reports.

**No mega-event in the period — growth was base-driven, which is the better kind.** FY26 (Apr 2025–Mar 2026) contained no World Cup or Euros; the FIFA World Cup 2026 (11 Jun–19 Jul 2026) falls entirely in FY27 Q1. A +6% year without an event tailwind implies underlying lottery/sports demand and online adoption are doing the work, and sets up an easier FY27 comparison.

**Horse racing: first full year with zero local racing.** Singapore Turf Club ceased local meetings in October 2024 (FY25 had ~6 months of Kranji racing); FY26 horse wagering was entirely overseas simulcast (Hong Kong, Australia, Japan, Korea, South Africa, UK via UK Tote commingling since Mar-24). Any product-level attrition was absorbed within the group total [product impact unverified].

**Cost base: investment programme, not a transformation programme.** No cost-reduction plan exists. FY25 opex rose 6.3% to S$353m (2.8% of turnover) on a transition to new-generation gaming systems, a new horse-racing broadcast studio and in-store AV upgrades. FY26 opex is unverified, but the flat Tote Board contribution against +6% turnover is consistent with opex growing faster than stakes [inference].

**Capital position is not applicable in the conventional sense.** The surplus is remitted to the Tote Board; there is no external equity, no public debt, no buyback and no dividend to third parties. The annual report publishes no balance sheet, cash flow or P&L — net debt, leverage, FCF and EPS are n/a by construction.

**Parent read-through.** The Tote Board Group (Tote Board + Singapore Pools + Singapore Turf Club) reported FY25 income of S$3.705bn (secondary source states +4% vs S$3.66bn, which does not reconcile arithmetically — flagged). Tote Board FY26 figures are not yet published; Singapore Pools' audited accounts sit inside the Tote Board report, not the Pools AR.

**Regulatory backdrop stable but tightening at the margin.** Regulated by the Gambling Regulatory Authority (since 2022); recertified at WLA Responsible Gaming Level 4. Management's stated priorities (FY24/25 ARs): customer retention and diversion from illegal operators, modernising the retail network, driving online adoption via the Singapore Pools Account. Watch safer-play measures on online account limits and advertising.

**Management continuity.** Chairman Kai S. Nargolwala and CEO Lam Chee Weng signed the FY25 joint message; the FY26 leadership statement could not be retrieved in this session [unverified]. No management change was reported by secondary sources.

**Thesis read-through for listed peers.** (a) Singapore's consumer gambling wallet is still compounding mid-single digits — supportive for Genting Singapore's mass segment and for lottery-monopoly comps (The Lottery Corp, Tabcorp, Allwyn) as evidence that monopoly lottery/tote turnover can grow 4–7% through the cycle at ~3% opex; (b) post-Kranji, Hong Kong and Australian racing bodies are the structural beneficiaries of Singapore simulcast demand; (c) duty-rate sensitivity: every 1pt of effective duty on S$13.5bn is ~S$135m, larger than any plausible opex saving.

**What management is emphasising vs burying.** Emphasised: record turnover, the 97% figure, community/CSR metrics. Not disclosed: product mix, online penetration, payout ratios by product, opex detail, and why the Tote Board contribution barely grew. A PM should treat the headline as fiscal data, not operating data.

**Data confidence: Medium.** Headline turnover, duties & taxes and Tote Board contribution are double-sourced (company website citing AR 2025/26 + Gaming Intelligence). FY26 prize payouts, opex, product/channel detail and management commentary are unverified — the AR 2025/26 PDF was not retrievable during research. Comparatives: AR 2023/24 (read in full) and four independent media reports of AR 2024/25.

segments.name: Group value chain — turnover to Tote Board contribution (single reportable entity)
segments.headline: +S$790m of incremental stakes: ~27c per dollar to duties, ~1c to the Tote Board, ~72c to prizes and opex — the surplus line did not participate in the growth.
narrative: They reported turnover of S$13.48bn for the year to 31 March 2026, up 6.2% on FY25's S$12.69bn and the third successive record; the company's own site rounds this to S$13.5bn and attributes it to the Annual Report 2025/26. Growth re-accelerated from the 4.0% posted in FY25 and sits just below FY24's 7.0%, giving a three-year compound rate of 5.7% off FY23's S$11.4bn base. What makes the number more interesting than the headline suggests is the calendar: the period contained no World Cup or Euros, local horse racing had already ceased, and GST was unchanged at 9% throughout, so there is no obvious event or policy lever to explain the step-up. We read it as underlying demand — most plausibly lottery jackpot cycles and continued migration to the Singapore Pools Account — though the company gives no product or channel split with which to test that.

The distribution of that turnover is where the year gets less flattering. Betting duties and taxes rose 9.2% to S$2.49bn, lifting the effective rate to 18.5% of stakes from 18.0%, while the contribution to the Tote Board — the closest thing this entity has to a profit line, since the surplus is remitted upward to its statutory-board parent — rose only 1.4% to S$583m, or 4.3% of turnover against 4.5% a year earlier. Put differently, of the S$790m of additional stakes, roughly S$210m went to the Exchequer, S$8m to the Tote Board and the remaining S$572m to prizes and operating costs. In FY25 the picture was the reverse: duties were flat (−0.4%) on 4% turnover growth and the Tote Board contribution jumped 32%. The two years together look like a mix swing — a sports/racing-weighted FY25 giving way to a lottery-weighted FY26, since lottery products carry the higher duty rate — but we flag this as inference; the annual report does not say.

Prize payouts and operating expenses for FY26 were not retrievable, so we work from the residual. Turnover less duties less the Tote Board contribution leaves S$10.41bn, which is 77.2% of stakes — exactly the FY25 ratio (S$9.45bn prizes plus S$353m opex on S$12.69bn). If opex grew in line with the FY25 trajectory (S$332m to S$353m, +6.3%) to roughly S$370–400m, prize payouts were about S$10.0bn and the payout ratio 74.2–74.5%, in line with FY25's 74.5% and FY24's 74.9%. On that basis implied gross win (turnover less prizes) was around S$3.45–3.47bn, up 6–7%, of which duties absorbed ~72% and the Tote Board contribution ~17%. Those are the ratios a PM should carry into any comparison with commercial operators: the state captures close to 88% of gross win before a single salary is paid, and the 3% opex ratio that management repeats each year is the only variable the company genuinely controls.

The company frames all of this as "97% returned to Singapore and Singaporeans" — prizes, duties and the Tote Board contribution combined — and the arithmetic holds again this year at roughly S$13.1bn on our derived figures, after S$12.3bn (97.0%) in FY25 and S$11.87bn (97.3%) in FY24. We would not over-interpret the stability: it is largely a function of a lottery-heavy payout ratio that is fixed by game design and a duty regime set by statute. The variable that should concern the Tote Board, as the beneficiary of the surplus, is that the contribution has gone from 3.6% of turnover in FY24 to 4.5% to 4.3%, and that the FY26 flatness coincides with a multi-year systems and retail investment programme whose cost is not separately disclosed.

No conventional capital metrics apply. There is no net debt, no leverage, no buyback and no external dividend; the balance sheet and cash flow are consolidated into the Tote Board's accounts, which are published separately and later. The relevant parent datapoint is Tote Board Group income of S$3.705bn for FY25 (comprising the Tote Board, Singapore Pools and the Singapore Turf Club); the FY26 equivalent is not yet available and would be the first place to look for the audited Pools P&L.

segments.name: Products & channels — Lottery (TOTO / 4D / Singapore Sweep), Sports betting, Horse racing; retail vs Singapore Pools Account
segments.headline: No product-level numbers are disclosed; qualitatively, FY26 was the first full year without local horse racing and without a mega football event, which makes the +6% group print more creditable than it looks.
narrative: They remain the sole legal operator of lotteries, sports betting and horse-race wagering in Singapore, with turnover generated from five products — TOTO, 4D and the Singapore Sweep on the lottery side, sports betting (football and motor racing) and horse racing — sold through a retail estate that at the last published count (FY24) comprised 84 branches, 3 Livewire venues, 9 off-course betting centres and 201 authorised retailers, plus the online Singapore Pools Account. None of the three product lines is reported separately in turnover, gross win or payout terms, and no actives, ARPU, handle, hold or promotional-intensity metrics exist in any filing. What follows is therefore the qualitative record from the FY24 and FY25 reports plus our own inference; FY26-specific product commentary could not be retrieved and is flagged as such.

On lottery, the historical pattern is that 4D and TOTO carry the bulk of stakes and the bulk of the duty burden, with sales calendars anchored on the TOTO Hongbao draw at Chinese New Year (which fell on 17 Feb 2026, inside FY26 Q4), the National Day special draw with an added second-half jackpot draw, and the S$5m Singapore Sweep jackpot around the Mid-Autumn festival. The FY26 duty line is the tell: duties & taxes grew 9% on 6% turnover growth, and the incremental duty rate of ~27c per S$1 is well above the 18c blended average, which is what one would expect if higher-duty lottery products grew faster than sports and racing. A large TOTO rollover cycle in the year would do exactly this, and would also explain why the payout ratio (derived ~74%) did not drift up despite the volume. We cannot verify the mix from the disclosures, and the company's core lottery system refresh (completed May 2023) should be treated as the operational enabler rather than the driver.

Sports betting is the product management has consistently described as the growth engine — the FY24 report cited "strong growth momentum due to new leagues and more sporting events" after adding six football leagues (including second-tier divisions in Germany, the Netherlands, Japan and Spain), new half-time/extra-time bet types, and a cash-out feature piloted on the A-League in November 2023 and extended thereafter. The FY26 calendar offered no Euros or World Cup; the FIFA Club World Cup (June–July 2025, US venues, Asia-unfriendly kick-off times) was the only non-domestic tournament of note. The absence of an event tailwind cuts both ways: it means FY26's 6% did not lean on sports, and it means FY27 Q1 (the expanded 48-team World Cup, 11 Jun–19 Jul 2026) is a genuine, if time-zone-impaired, step-up opportunity. The cash-out and content expansion are framed explicitly as a counter to illegal operators rather than as margin tools — pricing and promotional intensity are not levers the company discusses, and we would not model them.

Horse racing is the structurally impaired product. The Singapore Turf Club ran its last Kranji meeting in October 2024 after 182 years, so FY25 contained roughly six months of local racing and FY26 none; all wagering is now on overseas simulcasts, with the company having added jurisdictions (Saudi Arabia, Turkey, Germany) alongside the core Hong Kong, Australian, Japanese, Korean and South African cards, and having entered a commingling arrangement with the UK Tote in March 2024 to stabilise dividends on UK races. A new centralised betting control centre and a horse-racing broadcast studio were built to support this. The group-level +6% means any racing attrition was more than absorbed, but the duty and surplus arithmetic suggests the absorbing product was lottery, not sports — a less durable substitute. We would expect racing turnover to keep shrinking as the local fan base ages out without a home track.

On channels, management's stated priorities since FY24 have been customer retention and diversion from illegal online operators, modernising the retail network and driving online adoption through the Singapore Pools Account, which carries self-monitoring tools (My Gaming Profile) and sits under a dedicated Safer Play Workgroup aligned to Gambling Regulatory Authority obligations and the company's WLA Level 4 responsible-gaming recertification. Online penetration is not disclosed. The FY25 report flagged capital going into a new-generation gaming system transition and in-store audio-visual upgrades; opex rose 6.3% that year to S$353m, and the flat FY26 Tote Board contribution is most simply explained by that programme continuing to run ahead of turnover. There is no segment guidance; the only forward statement the company makes is its mandate to remain an effective counter to illegal operators while minimising gambling harm, which in practice caps how aggressively it can market or price.

forecast.intro: There is no guidance to bridge: Singapore Pools issues no forecasts, holds no earnings call and reports once a year. The bridge below therefore reconciles the reported FY25→FY26 movement and sets out our own FY27 (Apr 2026–Mar 2027) estimate. The FY26 delta was driven entirely by the group-level turnover line (no divisional data exists); the notable feature is that the S$790m of incremental stakes flowed ~27% to duties and ~1% to the Tote Board, with ~72% absorbed by prizes and operating costs — the inverse of FY25, when duties were flat and the Tote Board contribution captured ~28c of each incremental dollar.

bridge.title: FY26 state take: duties S$2.49bn + Tote Board S$583m
FY27E turnover (our estimate)
bridge.change: +4–7%; World Cup 2026 in Q1; no local racing drag to lap

forecast.view: **Turnover.** We model FY27E stakes of S$14.0–14.4bn (+4–7%). The base case is trend growth of 4–5% (≈S$14.0–14.15bn) plus a World Cup uplift we size at only 1–2pts (S$150–250m): the 2026 tournament is the largest ever (104 matches) but North American kick-off times fall between ~01:00 and ~11:00 SGT, which historically dampens live-betting engagement relative to Qatar's evening slots, and sports is the smaller product. FY24 grew 7% while lapping the Qatar World Cup year, which tells us the event sensitivity of the group total is modest. **Duties & taxes.** At an 18.3–18.5% effective rate, S$2.56–2.66bn (+3–7%); the swing factor is mix — a sports-led World Cup year would pull the blended rate back toward FY25's 18.0%. **Surplus/Tote Board contribution.** S$560–650m. The range is wide because opex is undisclosed: if the systems transition keeps opex growing ~6–8% (≈S$400–430m) and the payout ratio holds ~74.5%, the contribution is roughly flat-to-up 5%; if the programme rolls off, there is S$50m+ of upside. Lottery jackpot luck (TOTO rollover sequences) is the other unmodellable variable and can move the line by tens of millions either way. **Leverage.** Not applicable — the entity remains debt-free and remits its surplus; no change expected. **Key risks.** (1) Budget 2027 changes to betting duty rates (each 1pt on S$13.5bn ≈ S$135m, larger than any opex lever); (2) GRA safer-play measures on online account limits or advertising; (3) continued racing attrition post-Kranji; (4) illegal online operator leakage, which the company cannot counter with promotions. **Our stance on the print:** a solid volume year whose economics accrued to the Exchequer rather than the owner; the FY27 question is whether the surplus line re-couples to turnover once the investment cycle peaks. All FY27 figures are our estimates, not company guidance.
